definition: Embryonic means in an early and undeveloped stage.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word embryonic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know embryonic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The peace talks remain embryonic — after a month, the two delegations have agreed only on the shape of the table.
Budding goes past embryonic — the shape has broken the surface and anyone can watch it grow.
Full-blown is far stronger than embryonic: an embryonic plan is still a faint early sketch, while a full-blown one has gone all the way to its complete, finished form.

Undeveloped is the flat, factual word for what has not yet grown — no image behind it, no promise attached. Embryonic borrows the embryo's picture: the design already present, the parts barely sketched, growth clearly on the way. Call a district undeveloped and you describe it; call a plan embryonic and you bet on its future.

A fledgling has just left the nest — young and wobbly, but already out in the air. A fledgling venture is likewise up and working while it finds its wings. Embryonic is earlier still: formed enough to exist, too unformed to do anything yet.
development complete
every part already in its final shape

Embryonic came into English whole, from Greek embryon — en ('within') plus bryein ('to swell'). The swelling root bry- built nothing else in everyday English; apart from embryo itself, this word has no common relatives to recognize it by.
Embryonic means in an early and undeveloped stage.

In 1990 the country's democracy was embryonic: one independent newspaper run from a basement, a parliament that met in a gymnasium, a constitution that was still nine handwritten pages in a law professor's satchel.
Foreign observers counted institutions and found almost nothing — which was the point.
Almost nothing is what the earliest stage of anything looks like.
Embryonic is the exact word because it names what is in an early and undeveloped stage — formed enough to exist, too unformed to work at full size.
It leans on biology's picture of the embryo: the design present, the parts barely sketched.
Call a thing embryonic and you promise growth while admitting how little there is to show today.
Embryonic suits plans, movements, and ventures at the barely-formed stage, and it quietly promises growth to come.
Its opposite number in this unit is precocious, which praises a person for developing ahead of schedule — embryonic describes the thing itself, still barely begun.
For plain factual smallness with no growth implied, undeveloped is the flatter choice.

In March the plan to farm kelp off the point was embryonic: two pages of notes, a borrowed depth chart, and a list of permits no one had applied for.
Nothing about it could yet touch the water.
The ropes existed only as a sketch, the buoys only as a line in a budget that had no money in it.
Still, the shape of the whole operation was visible in those notes — anchor lines here, harvest skiff there, drying shed on the old cannery floor.
By August the first ropes were wet, and by the next spring the crew was selling kelp to two restaurants in town.
The harbormaster keeps the original two pages pinned to her wall, because nothing on them had to be crossed out — only built.
